speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Under the Constitution, the President is the Head of State.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: As the Head of State, the President performs a vital symbolic and unifying role.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: He symbolises our sovereignty at home and abroad, and is an important part of our international diplomacy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In performing these roles, Presidents have, from time to time, taken on additional appointments in their official capacities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is done on the advice and with the support of the Cabinet.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For example, domestically, Presidents have served as university chancellors and patrons of charitable or other organisations, lending the prestige of the highest office of the land to worthy causes that unify Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Internationally, Presidents can take on appointments in their official capacity in furtherance of Singapore’s national interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For example, Dr Tony Tan was inducted as a member of the Honorary Senate of the Foundation Lindau Nobel Laureate Meetings in 2012 during his tenure as President.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Such appointments reflect the high international standing of the individuals who have served as our President.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Cabinet will continue to apply these principles in deciding whether to advise and support the President to take on domestic and international appointments in his official capacity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Today, President Tharman is the Chancellor of the National University of Singapore and Nanyang Technological University, and patron of numerous organisations like the Singapore Red Cross, Singapore International Foundation, Philanthropy Asia Alliance and the Singapore University of Social Sciences.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: President Tharman is also currently holding the following international positions in his official capacity as President, with the advice and support of the Cabinet, and these are: One, Chairman of the Board of Trustees of the Group of Thirty (G30).

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This oversees the governance and directions of the G30, which is a grouping of eminent thought leaders in economic policymaking, academia and the financial industry.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Two, Member of the Board of Trustees of the World Economic Forum (WEF).

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It helps shape the strategic directions of the WEF without directly overseeing the running of the organisation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Three, Co-chair of the Global Commission on the Economics of Water (GCEW).

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is an independent Commission that was convened to examine and make recommendations to the United Nations (UN) and other international forums on how to improve the way societies govern, use and value water for the common good.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Four, Co-chair of the United Nations Human Development Report (UNHDR) Advisory Board.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This provides intellectual guidance and advice on the overall vision, direction and messages of the UN HDR.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These are appointments that President Tharman held when he was Senior Minister and before assuming his current office.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The four international bodies mentioned earlier want their distinguished appointees to carry on with their official roles, and to bring with them their official status and reputations, such as President Tharman’s former status as Senior Minister and now as Head of State.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These international organisations want their distinguished appointees to carry with them their official statuses, but they also want their appointees to contribute independently to achieve the aims of the respective bodies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: To illustrate, the WEF Board of Trustees includes the deputy prime minister of Canada, the heads of the World Trade Organization (WTO), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank, and leaders of major private organisations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: But these Trustees are expected to give their views independent of the governments or organisations they head, so as to shape the strategic directions of the WEF in keeping with its goals of serving the interests of the global community.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Similarly, the G30’s Board of Trustees includes current and former heads of central banks around the world, but they are expected to contribute independently of these central banks.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Likewise, the UNHDR Advisory Board and the GCEW expect their members to contribute independently, in the global interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: If the President were to serve in these international bodies purely in his official capacity, then he would be limited to representing the official Singapore position in everything he says.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: That would not be in keeping with the requirements of these organisations, nor would it be in the interest of Singapore for our President to be so limited, as it restricts our ability to shape global conversations and initiatives.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: From Singapore’s perspective, there is value to have the President represented on these international bodies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It enables us to be plugged into global conversations and to understand and help shape the thinking that takes place in these important and influential international bodies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: But for this to happen, the President must be able to function credibly in these international bodies, by lending his expertise to advance the agenda on broader issues of concern to these organisations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: So, we are presented with a novel issue: should the President now be allowed to contribute independently in his private capacity when he takes on these international appointments?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These are reputable international bodies with global reach, and with eminent persons serving on their respective boards.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The President’s continued involvement in these organisations is in Singapore’s national interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: To be clear, when we say that the President serves in his “private capacity”, it does not mean that he is doing this outside of his work duties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These international appointments are core to the President’s international diplomacy role.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: As Head of State, they are, in fact, how we project Singapore’s influence and strengthen our networks in the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: But allowing the President to serve in his private capacity allows him to act independently in achieving the aims of the international bodies, subject, of course, to the necessary safeguards of our national interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Such an arrangement would then enable the President to take on appointments that help to expand Singapore’s influence and network, while acting independently on these international bodies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: And that is why constitutional amendments are needed to enable the President to take on roles where he acts independently in his private capacity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The provisions in this amendment Bill will put in place a proper framework under which these and future appointments are governed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The framework would not just apply to this President and this Government, but also to future Presidents and future Governments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In developing the framework, Cabinet had regard to the following broad considerations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: One, the framework would only apply to appointments in international organisations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It would not apply in the domestic context.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In the domestic context, the current position will continue to apply, and the President will not have an independent role outside of the specific discretionary powers conferred on him by the Constitution.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Two, any international appointment for the President to act in his private capacity must be justified by the national interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Importantly, our own policy matters must remain the responsibility and prerogative of the Cabinet.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Any appointment must therefore be supported by the Cabinet in the first place.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: If need be, Cabinet must be able to intervene to advise the President on how he acts in these appointments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Three, at the same time, the President should have a say in deciding whether to take on such appointments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: He should be able to decline such appointments if, for example, he considers them to be incompatible with his constitutional functions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: And any appointment must be on the public record, in the interests of transparency and accountability.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: First, the President cannot contravene the disabilities imposed by Article 19A(1), which include a prohibition on active engagement in commercial enterprises.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Second, the Cabinet must assess and advise the President that it is in the national interest for the President to accept the appointment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In making this assessment, Cabinet would be guided by similar principles as those I set out earlier.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Third, the President, acting in his discretion, must concur with the advice of the Cabinet.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The President cannot accept an international appointment in his private capacity outside of the framework set out in this Article.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Article 22Q(2) will enable the Cabinet to advise the President on his execution of such a role so that it is in our national interest, including ensuring that it does not undermine the President’s status as constitutional Head of State or contradict the President’s powers under the Constitution.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The President must act in accordance with any such advice.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Subject to any advice by the Cabinet, the President may act independently in his private capacity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Article 22Q(3) goes on to require the President to relinquish an international appointment if so advised by the Cabinet.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: And finally, Article 22Q(4) requires the acceptance or the relinquishment of an international appointment to be published in the Gazette.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This Gazette notice will include the term dates of the appointment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Conceptually, the new Article 22Q will be a specific and defined extension of the President’s international role as the Head of State.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It is not part of the Elected President’s custodial powers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: But, in fact, we do not need this backdating.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Because, as I mentioned earlier, President Tharman currently holds his appointments in an official capacity, on the advice and support of the Cabinet, as provided for in the Constitution.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Today, Ministers take on external appointments in their official capacity in connection with their responsibilities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For example, when Singapore was a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council, Prof S Jayakumar, as the Minister for Foreign Affairs then, served as the President of the Council.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Code of Conduct for Ministers also permits Ministers to take on external appointments in their private capacities if the Prime Minister considers it to be in the national interest and grants permission.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Currently, Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean sits on the TotalEnergies’ International Advisory Committee.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This appointment was approved by the Prime Minister and was published in the Gazette.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Senior Minister Teo donates the honorarium he receives from TotalEnergies to charity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: There are no general legal impediments to Ministers taking on external appointments today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: However, as we are putting a legal framework in place for the President to take on international appointments in his private capacity, we will also create a legal framework for Ministers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is found in the new Article 33A.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: As a general rule, Ministers taking on international appointments in their private capacities will be instructed against breaching collective Cabinet responsibility; against making any commitments on behalf of the Government of Singapore, whether formally or informally; and against retaining any remuneration or benefits in connection with the appointment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: I should add that the new Article 33A does not apply to the Prime Minister.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Previous and current Prime Ministers have not undertaken any such international appointments, and we do not expect future Prime Ministers to do so.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Hence, the provision in the new Article 33A only applies to Ministers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The proposed additions of Articles 22Q and 33A in the Constitution seek to ensure that we safeguard the dignity and status of the roles of the President and Ministers in Singapore, while enabling them to make significant contributions in international bodies and shape global thinking, if these contributions are in the interest of Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In this way, we can make the most of the expertise, experience and personal standing of the individuals we elect to office, so as to advance Singapore’s interests and reinforce our value to the world.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I will now present three compelling reasons to support this Bill, and then raise four common concerns, to which I seek the Deputy Prime Minister's response.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Three reasons to support the Bill: one, enhanced international influence.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, granting the President and Cabinet Ministers the opportunity to take on external roles, albeit in their personal and private capacity, can boost Singapore's visibility and status internationally.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore, as a small nation state, is often recognised for its effective governance and economic and social development.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Our leaders can offer essential insights for achieving progress and stability, beneficial to global policy-thinking and global policy-making.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Foreign and international organisations present an excellent platform for small nation states, like Singapore, to actively participate in shaping global policies, which may in turn affect Singapore positively.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And this was what the Deputy Prime Minister said about plugging into global conversations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, not every international organisation is formal or has the resources to appoint leaders in their official state roles.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, our collective support for our senior leaders to join these organisations, when it aligns with national interests, is crucial and strategic.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, President Tharman's significant contributions to entities, such as the IMF, the G20 Eminent Persons Group on Global Financial Governance, the Global Commission on the Economics of Water (GCEW) and so on, have positively impacted our nation's reputation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: President Tharman's continued involvement will offer valuable perspectives on global policymaking, which is especially beneficial for Singapore during these challenging economic and geopolitical times.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: During the last presidential election, there was widespread opinion that it would be a loss if Mr Tharman's ascent to the presidency hindered his international contributions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But President Tharman is not the only one whose insights are valued globally.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong, for example, has also frequently represented Singapore globally, enhancing our country's visibility, influence and reputation on the world stage.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And so have other public office holders; we heard about Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean, for instance.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, supporting this Bill is strategic and will offer Singapore the opportunity to punch above its weight, influencing global thinking and policymaking.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The second reason for supporting this Bill is the establishment of a framework, the creation of a formal framework, to prevent potential abuse.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Cabinet must advise the President that the appointment is in Singapore's national interest; and also against saying or doing anything against Singapore, in performing that role.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Third, this Bill encourages a shift in mindset from individual success to significance for our senior public leaders and nation alike.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Already, the Government has an existing practice of encouraging senior public servants to engage in non-commercial roles in their private capacity, fostering civic engagement and volunteerism.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Movement for the Intellectually Disabled of Singapore (MINDS), for example, a large charity for the intellectually challenged, has Permanent Secretary Augustin Lee as Chairman.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Where I volunteer, in the autism charities, Deputy Permanent Secretary Poon Hong Yuen provides invaluable insights on our Boards.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, when senior public office holders, such as Presidents and Ministers, contribute beyond their formal roles, and extend their expertise and experience globally, they too move the needle, from individual success to significance, benefiting wider communities and nations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I will next touch on four common concerns that are raised when the public, for example, read about this Bill.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, the first concern relates to the potential impact on the President and Cabinet Ministers' official duties.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some people worry that engaging in international roles in their private capacity may divert their attention from the elected and appointed responsibilities of the President and Ministers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister has shared some background to why this is happening and mentioned about international diplomacy in the President's role in such a case, but exactly what is the tipping point when one's overseas engagements are perceived as excessive?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, guidelines from the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) will be necessary to strike a suitable balance between the public and private roles of the President and the Ministers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The second concern is how the Prime Minister and Cabinet Ministers will determine the potential benefits of these roles to the country.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: While it is an honour to be invited to key positions in foreign organisations, not all roles may serve Singapore's interests.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, an objective assessment approach should be adopted to weigh the tangible benefits and drawbacks.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What is the meaning of "serving national interest"?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What are some examples of what might be beneficial or not quite beneficial to the nation?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some clarity in decision-making criteria and assessment weightage would be appreciated from the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The third concern is advising the Prime Minister under a similar situation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I know that the Deputy Prime Minister spoke about how current and past Prime Ministers do not have roles beyond their official duties in foreign and international organisations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But when such a situation happens, how would we move forward in this?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, if the Prime Minister himself is invited to hold office in a foreign or international organisation in a private capacity, what will happen?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It will be useful for the Deputy Prime Minister to clarify that.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is, hence, a fourth concern pertaining to the need for at least basic security and administrative support, even as one tries to distinguish between official and private engagements for the President and Cabinet Ministers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, while operational challenges may arise, and notwithstanding my seeking clarification for some of the concerns that I have raised, I am confident that they can be addressed through transparency, accountability and a commitment to serving the public interest.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And therefore, I stand in support of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The PMO asserts that such appointments can enhance Singapore's international standing and help to advance our national interest.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister said in his Second Reading speech that he is on all these boards in his official capacity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Internationally, it is a common practice for political office holders to resign from their private positions before being sworn into office.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Recently, Mr David Cameron resigned from various business and charitable positions, including as president of Alzheimer’s Research UK, when he made a comeback to government, saying, "I have one job – to be foreign secretary and work with the prime minister for the UK to be as secure and prosperous as possible in a difficult and dangerous world." Conversely, there are many examples of former politicians who are now leading high profile international bodies, but only started serving in these organisations after their political tenure in their home countries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Examples include Mr Antonio Guterres, the current Secretary-General of the United Nations, who was a former prime minister of Portugal, and Mr Charles Michel, who became the President of the European Council after stepping down as the Belgian prime minister.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The presence of currently serving Senior Public Officials in international organisations has led to controversies in the past.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In 2018, the European Union Ombudsman called on the then-European Central Bank (ECB) President Mario Draghi to resign from the G30, the same organisation whose Board of Trustees President Tharman is now Chairing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: She said, "Mr Draghi's membership of the G30 could give rise to a public perception that the independence of the ECB could be compromised".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Adding that, "For the ECB to allow this perception to arise over several years constitutes mal-administration on its part." The PMO stated that, from time to time, the President or Ministers are invited to take up key positions in foreign and international organisations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Prior to this, did any of our past Presidents assume positions in foreign organisations in their private capacities while they were still in office, or is Mr Tharman the first?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Additionally, have there been other invitations extended to the President for positions in foreign and international organisations that he has not yet accepted?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Could the Deputy Prime Minister provide the House a comprehensive list of his external commitments, both present and potential, so that Parliament can ascertain the extent of the President's involvement in these organisations and his expected annual time commitments for these roles?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Prior to his election, Mr Tharman articulated his vision for the presidency, emphasising the need for a different character to the Presidency in Singapore's next phase of development.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: He underscored the role of the President in checking the governance system, fostering unity and evolving Singapore's norms and culture.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: During his inauguration, he committed to using his mandate to strengthen multiracialism and enhance respect among communities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: His plans include promoting interaction between different communities, ensuring cultural vibrancy and fostering inclusivity through active community participation, civil society and support for the arts and sports.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are substantial commitments that will demand a significant investment of the President's time and effort.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: All of us – including the President – have only 24 hours each day.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Any time he spends serving private interests will be time taken away from his national duties to his constituents – who are the people of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Surely, the role of the President is significant enough to merit his undivided attention.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is a substantial amount of taxpayer money.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is only reasonable for Singaporeans to expect that he dedicates all his time and energy in his official capacity to meeting his promises to the people.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must more closely examine how these private roles, separate from official duties, genuinely advance Singapore's national interests.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How will the Government ensure that the President, when acting in his private capacity, follows the Cabinet's advice about what to say or do in his role, since many of these organisations hold their meetings behind closed doors in foreign countries?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister said just now that international organisations would want our President to continue in his official role.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They also want their appointees to contribute independently.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But if the Cabinet can instruct the President what to say or not to say, how is that contributing independently?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Invoking the "national interest" cannot grant the Government unrestricted authority to pursue its every desire.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, Singaporeans justifiably expect him to wholeheartedly dedicate his time and energy to fulfil his national responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Speaker, Sir, we are certainly feeling proud as a Singaporean when our then-Senior Minister Tharman was invited and appointed to serve at prestigious international organisations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He was appointed to Chair the G20 Eminent Persons Group on Global Financial Governance.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He also Chaired the Board of Trustees at the G30 and so on.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The jobs of our President and Ministers, who are also Members of Parliament (MPs) with constituency duties, are demanding.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While it may be beneficial for our national interest to have them appointed in foreign and international organisations and champion for Singapore, the concern is whether the demands of these appointments will have a negative impact on their ability to fulfil their local ones.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of Singapore's greatest challenges is our small pool of top local citizen talent which the Public Service, political and private sectors need to compete for.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps, one of the intents of this Bill is to overcome the constraints.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can understand that foreign and international organisations have their reasons for inviting the Ministers or the President.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If they should take these on, they might have to let go of other appointments to ensure that they have the time and energy to fulfil their main responsibilities as Ministers and MPs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is easy for the international arena to ignore tiny nations like us.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to have a presence wherever possible.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill also appears to address, urgently, the circumstances of the President since his inauguration on 14 September 2023.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: President Tharman is extremely respected by and popular among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He has brought honour to Singapore with his international achievements.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Personally, I have great respect for him, and it was my honour to have worked with him briefly in the mid-1980s when I was an Investment Officer at GIC and he was an Economist at the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the objections that I will raise in this speech have nothing to do with President Tharman personally or his international appointments specifically.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Rather, they arise from this Bill's violation of established legal principles and principles of sound governance, which I will move on now to elaborate on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, under Article 19A of the Constitution, the President is not allowed to hold any other office created or recognised by this Constitution, actively engage in any commercial enterprise, be a member of any political party or be a Member of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Constitution is silent on whether the President can take up foreign or international appointments.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But President Tharman has been holding such appointments when he was a Minister, before he was elected as the President.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other Ministers have also held international appointments over the years without question, despite the Constitution also being silent on this matter.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The most notable example was Mr Lee Kuan Yew who sat on the JP Morgan International Council while he was Minister Mentor.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, why is it so pressing to rush through these constitutional amendments now and create this framework for the President and Cabinet Ministers to take up international appointments?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it simply because no other past President had held international appointments in their private capacity while in office?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, then the Government should explain why there was no rush to create such a framework when a Minister took up foreign or international appointments for the first time many years ago.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second question the Government has to clarify is: why is it necessary for these constitutional amendments to be rushed through Parliament and backdated?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Constitution is the bedrock of our nation and any changes to it should be made with prudent consideration, transparency and in the best interest of only the nation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The constitutional amendments that we are debating today were brought to this House for First Reading less than three weeks ago and Parliament has been recalled today specifically to approve this fait accompli.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The retrospective amendment of any law should not be taken lightly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some other Singaporeans believe that the Government is establishing this framework to control what the President can or cannot say internationally under the new Article 22Q, clause 2.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Either way, this has tarnished the elected presidency.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans wonder, if any other person had been elected President, would the Government have enacted these constitutional amendments?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a universally recognised principle of good governance that situations of conflict of interest should be avoided as much as possible, in order to maintain the integrity of public institutions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While such situations cannot be totally eliminated, the Constitution should certainly not be amended to enable such situations to arise.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the President or Minister is truly acting in his private capacity, why then would the national interest be involved?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not easy, or might even be impossible, to ensure that one capacity does not lead to advantage in the other.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Constitution can be amended to enable the President and Ministers to take up foreign or international appointments of an executive nature, as opposed to mere ceremonial roles, an important question would arise – where does the buck stop?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What more is permissible or impermissible or what principles or guidelines would such decisions be based on?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, PSP is of the view that it is better for the President and Ministers to devote themselves entirely to their public offices in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As for these other international or foreign appointments, PSP is confident that there are other Singaporean talents suited for them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If President Tharman's foreign and international appointments are not unconstitutional, then it is perplexing why the amendments need to be backdated or even made at all, given that Cabinet Ministers have taken up such appointments over the years without such a framework and without any question of their legality and constitutionality.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, some Singaporeans believe that the Government has pushed through these amendments to strengthen its control over what the President says and does abroad.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Certainly, this issue of a president accepting and holding office in a foreign or international organisation in his private capacity has not been brought up for discussion in Parliament until today.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am also not aware of there being other elected heads of state elsewhere in the world who are allowed to hold any concurrent positions in foreign and international organisations in their private capacities while they are in office.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: President Tharman himself noted, when he was a presidential candidate, that the demands of the office have grown in the face of profound global risks and uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My colleague, the hon Member for Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC), Mr Gerald Giam, has shared with us earlier how President Tharman has articulated his vision for the presidency during his presidential campaign, including the roles he had expected to play and the work he had expected to carry out.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Suffice to say, the roles and work he has envisaged are very substantial and will take time and effort.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But every person, including all heads of state and our own Head of State, the President, only has 24 hours a day.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Whether the President has enough time is just one consideration.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Ought the President be allowed to do so is another question altogether.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The roles he is holding in international organisations do show that he is held by many with high regard and respect.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I can also agree with the Government’s argument that such positions can possibly enhance Singapore’s international standing and help to advance our national interest.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, the time spent on serving foreign and international organisations, no matter how fruitful they can be for our President and even for Singapore, equates to time not spent on his presidential responsibilities, including the roles he had campaigned on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: From the conversations I have had, I think there is a very strong argument for a serving president to concentrate wholeheartedly in his or her presidential responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In fact, undistracted by other external private responsibilities, our president can be encouraged to serve our country and people more fully, not unlike the way President Tharman has shared in his campaign.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some safeguards may well be necessary if this Bill is to be passed to expressly allow the President to hold an office in a foreign or international organisation in a private capacity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But are the proposed safeguards sufficient or ever sufficient?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will the proposed safeguards create other complications or unintended outcomes?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Yes, the Cabinet may be able to ask the President to relinquish his responsibility under Article 22Q(3).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, it may also be conceivable to argue that, at a time of crisis for such an international organisation or the community it serves, it may be morally or as a matter of conscience, difficult to step down and walk away from such a position of leadership.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If done, it may even affect the standing of our President or our country.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But if the President does not walk away and the Cabinet does not require him to relinquish, whether rightly or wrongly, it may still add to the time and responsibilities of the President within this foreign or international organisation which may, in turn, reduce or affect the time or attention he has on his actual role as our President.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: An example of potential conflicts of interest situation with the President assuming board or leadership positions on foreign or international organisations would be when such organisations were to, after our President’s appointment, hold certain views or may introduce policy reforms or changes in conventions where some such changes may not be completely acceptable to our Government or are inconsistent with our policies; being compelled to not speak up within that organisation, or even to resign at that point in time, may not look impressive to our international friends.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What are the remedies when an actual case of conflict of interest were to happen?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In comparison, the Ministerial Code provides that a breach of the Code can result in a Minister’s removal from office.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Also, what would be the recourse under the law if a President were to disagree with the Cabinet and does not step down for whatever reasons he may have?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Bill is silent on whether time and expenses incurred in the course of attending to the President’s duties in the foreign or international organisations in his private capacity would be strictly regarded as private and personal, since the appointments were made in his private capacity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will taxpayers have to foot the bill for the travel and accommodation expenses of the President and that of his support staff and even the security detail from the Istana?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What about the salaries of these civil servants?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Bill is also silent on the right of the President to accept remuneration from the foreign or international organisation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will the President, in his private capacity, have to take a leave of absence when attending to meetings of such foreign or international organisations in his private capacity?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, my questions above are also for the amendments in the proposed Article 33A pertaining to Ministers holding appointments in foreign and international organisations in their private capacity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would be grateful for the Deputy Prime Minister’s clarifications on the above as they relate to the use of taxpayers’ monies and the proper conduct of Government officials.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Allowing the President to take up appointments with foreign or international organisations in his private capacity could detract from his official Presidential duties.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I agree that having our men and women on the seats of these bodies will be highly beneficial to Singapore in providing the opportunity to present our perspectives, shape discourse and advance our national interests.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Having a seat at the table makes a difference to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we cast our eyes overseas, there are example of ministers from other countries who are part of international organisations.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, Canada's deputy prime minister and minister of finance, Ms Chrystia Freeland, and Rwanda's minister of information communication technology and innovation, Ms Paula Ingabire, are members of WEF's Board of Trustees.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a small island state with no natural resources, Singapore has thrived due to its people's capabilities and their connectivities with our global partners.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need to continue to promote Singapore well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Indeed, the appointments of our leaders to such institutions will enhance Singapore's visibility and international standing, which include intangible qualities which have tangible and significant impact on our development and progress as a nation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Parliament should have more clarity on this issue.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What happens if they put forth views not representative of, or even contrary to, the Government at these meetings?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How do we separate the stances of the private individuals from the office they hold?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): In addition, what would be the criteria set by the Cabinet for the organisations to be deemed acceptable?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will there be any control over the type and number of organisations that the President and Ministers may participate in?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What are the guidelines that determine which roles may be approved?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will the Government ensure that these individuals will not take on too many roles which may have a detrimental impact on their ability to fulfil the requirements of their main jobs?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would also like to ask how different are these international roles from the non-executive ones, such as patrons, which our President and Ministers undertake concurrently?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, President Tharman is the Patron of the Digital for Life Movement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will focus my remarks on clause 1.2 of the Bill, notably, the retrospective dating of stipulations to September 2023.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I appreciate that Deputy Prime Minister Wong has indicated earlier that the backdating was not necessary per se but introduced it out of an abundance of caution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, for me, this is even more worrisome, for reasons that would become evident over the course of my speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Retrospective applications of the law, sometimes referred to as retrospective or ex post facto laws, involve backdating the legal status of actions undertaken prior to the enactment of the law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Legislative retrospectivity may affect previously established legal relationships and rights and may attach new legal consequences to earlier decisions made by parties that did not anticipate these consequences under prior law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Ex post facto laws are, indeed, permissible in Westminster-style parliamentary systems such as ours because of the principle of parliamentary supremacy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet even legislative sovereignty must be located within the legal order where the rule of law remains absolute.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Whether one subscribes to a thicker or thinner conception of the rule of law, the general principle that laws should be prospective, open and clear is not contested.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we routinely amend laws and apply them after the fact, then we erode the very stability of the rule of law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These are consequences not just for the institution of the rule of law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Retroactive laws compromise both efficiency as well as equity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: You can also, in the words of our own Court of Appeal, "undermine expectations".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Retroactivity becomes especially thorny when applied to matters involving the Constitution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Constitutions are meant to embody deep, fundamental principles that form the legal basis for the governance of sovereign countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, in many jurisdictions worldwide, constitutions or Bill of rights form the very basis for prohibitions on retroactive legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This includes Brazil, Indonesia, Iran, Ireland, Italy, Japan, New Zealand, Norway, the Philippines and Russia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even in countries when the constitution does not explicitly prohibit ex post facto laws, they are almost always circumscribed, especially for criminal law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Retroactive legislation enacted elsewhere has also been challenged on constitutional grounds, often at the very highest levels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the last session of Parliament, this House was very careful about enshrining specific provisions and rights into the Constitution precisely because of the notion that matters of policy that may not be sufficiently enduring should not garner constitutional amendments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It stands that we wish to be very careful about introducing retroactive clauses into any constitutional amendments because doing so would open up avenues for other future changes that could likewise be dated retroactively.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since the RSIA has constitutional significance, this clearly justifies its retroactive application.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another has to do with certain Bills related to pensions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Pensions Act, enacted in 1956, was retroactively set to commence in 1939.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Amendments to the Parliamentary Pensions Act were made retroactive from the commencement of the original Act, and the Act to eventually abolish such pensions was likewise rendered operative a little than a year earlier, relative to when it was passed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This retroactive applicability was to align either with when the principal Act come into operation or with actual practice, when pensions had already been frozen since May 2011.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is, again, justifiable since the nature of pensions is such that they are accrued incrementally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The most recent example is in the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Certain parts of the Act, notably on conducting in-person meetings, were backdated to March that year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given the limited understanding surrounding a novel and deadly disease, it is reasonable to expect the need to predate policy changes made in the fog of a life-and-death battle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, Mr Speaker, there have been other instances where retroactivity was applicable but not hardcoded into the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Section 8D of the Internal Security Act embeds a commencement provision that applies the amendments to proceedings that predate the Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Amendments to the Singapore Military Forces Act, which affected reservists, were also ante-dated to two years prior, to be consistent with the functions assigned to the then Defence Forces Record Officer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As suggested earlier, this basic argument should hold with even greater force when we are looking at a constitutional amendment, lest we run afoul of the underlying principles that undergird the rule of law as embodied in the highest law of the land.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nevertheless, we are left with an uncomfortable position of asking ourselves whether the stipulations of the proposed constitutional amendments rise to the level of the sort of circumstances spelt out in the prior instances where legislative retroactivity was accommodated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The stipulations in today's Bill only serve to reinforce that fear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, if one deems the matters raised by this Bill as sufficiently serious, why were they not considered for passage previously?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, the PMO statement on the Bill suggests that invitations to the President or Ministers to take on international roles arise "from time to time".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, why was this sort of accommodation not previously drafted into prospective law rather than now, retroactively, and as a constitutional amendment no less?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If it was prior to the most recent presidential election, could our present need to pass a retroactive law have been avoided with a law that was enacted earlier instead of seemingly taking the passage of the constitutional amendment for granted?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And, if so, why was this matter of the President taking on or retaining such extracurricular appointments not clearly identified as an election issue so that the electorate would be able to make more informed voting choices when they cast their vote?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Or is it bordering on an abuse of the Parliamentary supermajority to effect constitutional amendments of this nature at will?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We may be a small nation, but Singapore has gained international respect and admiration in several areas since our founding.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The world today is yet again facing a series of challenges.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: After recovering from the Global Financial Crisis of 2008 with seeming peace and financial stability, COVID-19 hit.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I use "seeming peace" because there were still areas of conflict and, if those were not contained, could have certainly brought global disruptions.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Geopolitical tensions between the United States (US) and China have deepened, although there may seem to be some ray of hope recently, and Russia invaded Ukraine in early 2022, triggering political and economic fallout.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Regionally, we are seeing the continuing issues in Myanmar.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Most recently, we are witnessing the Israel-Hamas war, with ripples through racial and religious communities despite statements that this is neither a racial nor a religious conflict.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's domestic well-being depends on regional and global well-being.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: As a country dependent on regional and global peace and prosperity, we cannot look the other way when and where events occur that impact trade, financial systems, peace and global order.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This, of course, must also include the ongoing efforts to address the urgent needs concerning climate change and the environment.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed amendments may seem like a couple of sentences.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: But the potential impact will likely be much more.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I refer to potential positive impact on a regional and global scale.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: And I believe, harnessed wisely, this will, in turn, reap positive impact for us domestically.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Our founding Prime Minister, Mr Lee Kuan Yew, put Singapore on the world map despite our small nation status.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: He was supported by a capable and able strong team, as he often acknowledged.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: He also made it a practice to bring younger leaders along with him to observe, listen and learn.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: After handing over political leadership, Mr Lee remained highly sought after internationally for his advice, his views and his outlook on a whole range of matters.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: He also concurrently provided guidance and advice when requested on domestic matters.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Global institutions continue to be dominated by the global powers.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Often, this comes down to fundamental dominance by size and funding.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Global institutions, though, are also facing the risk of losing relevance.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There are many different views why this is the case.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Despite this, it would be against our interests to ever feel that we, as a small nation, cannot contribute.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It may take time, effort, persuasion, trust, cultivating relationships.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: If our leaders are invited to perform foreign and international roles in their private capacities, we should, therefore, encourage this if this is in our national interest.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The recent rapid increase in interest rates from a decade of almost zero interest may continue to test the global economic fabric.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Stock markets remain volatile and rise and fall in anticipation of whether the US Federal Reserve will increase interest rates.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The ability to navigate the global financial uncertainty in the coming years will need the best minds and, of course, sound fiscal policy.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This is all happening at a time when global trade is becoming increasingly protective.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We, therefore, need to protect our future interests, both domestically and internationally.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: And we have been doing so and we must continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: As our leaders with sharp minds, expertise and experience debate and discuss issues of importance at international forums, we play our part in contributing to global solutions and actions.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Participation at international forums will also be a channel where we remain open to learning from others and, perhaps, bringing back lessons that may improve our own policies and practices.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I trust our leaders will be bringing along younger leaders to observe, listen and learn.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Our private and people sectors have also contributed on the global stage over the decades.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It may be timely to see whether more public, private and people sector collaboration may be beneficial in selected global arenas.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: As a financial hub, we will have gained much private sector knowledge and expertise and continue to attract a significant amount of funds under management.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We have also gained significant experience in establishing and stewarding our Sovereign Wealth Funds.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore International Foundation (SIF) has been mobilising the people sector in cross-border engagement.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Social entrepreneurs emerging from this programme have brought positive impact and change to a whole spectrum of communities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: If the SDGs are achieved, the world should be in a better place.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me, Mr Speaker, to conclude with this well-known quote from Mr Lee Kuan Yew: "For the young, let me tell you the sky has turned brighter.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There is a glorious rainbow that beckons those with the spirit of adventure.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: And there are rich findings at the end of the rainbow.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: To the young and to the not-so-old, I say, look at that horizon, follow that rainbow, go ride it." I cling onto the few words that say, "not-so-old".

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The distinction between whether the President or the Minister is acting in the capacity of a Singaporean officeholder or a foreign one is important.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially considering the potential for perceptions that they are still acting as officeholders even in a private capacity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will it be apparent as to whom the President or Minister represents when wearing these different hats?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The potential switching between roles raises concerns about the clarity of representation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The public must be able to discern whether the President or Minister is acting on behalf of Singapore, the foreign organisation or both.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we ensure that individuals holding these roles align with our national priorities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there restrictions on the types of organisations that they can serve in?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is the President and are the Ministers prohibited from serving on foreign bodies, even remotely, if the foreign organisation's agenda poses a conflict of interest?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This consideration is paramount in preventing Singapore's officeholders from using privileged information gained from their positions or accidentally disclosing official secrets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Another key consideration is the connection that exposes them to vulnerabilities that cybercriminals may exploit.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Were there prohibitions in place before the appointment as President?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Do the amendments apply to the appointments made before the role of the President was assumed?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I ask these questions because if the constitutional amendments are made retrospectively, it would be a practice not commonly observed in legislative amendments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Speaker, Sir, I am concerned about the potential impact on the President's and the Ministers' abilities to fulfil their duties to the nation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With this amendment, are we confident that they will have sufficient time and bandwidth to execute their roles in both the external organisation and their official capacities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is there a time limit for serving in these foreign or international organisations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Who bears the expenses associated with travel for these appointments?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Besides the monetary aspects, it touches upon the very image and perception of the office.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How palatable would it be for the President to receive full wages alongside additional remuneration for a secondary appointment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Participation in international organisations provides our leaders with an exceptional platform to establish diplomatic connections with influential leaders across diverse nations and sectors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These networks can translate into collaborations and partnerships that ultimately benefit Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such appointments also provide the opportunity to showcase their expertise at an international level.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This not only elevates their personal standing but further amplifies the influence and reputation of our nation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These international roles often involve addressing pressing global challenges, such as climate change.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our leaders, in such capacities, can contribute to meaningful solutions on a broader and international scale.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In addition, by actively participating in international organisations, our leaders become effective advocates for Singapore's interests on a global stage.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This may encompass negotiations on international agreements and influencing global policies in favour of our nation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Hence, achieving a balance among these diverse roles, all the while steadfastly prioritising Singapore's national interests, is critical.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In doing so, we would allow for the optimal utilisation of our leaders' skills on both the domestic and international fronts, ultimately contributing to the advancement of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My clarifications notwithstanding, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have listened to the speeches of the Opposition Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are entitled to their views, but I take a very divergent view.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my view, the amendments are fundamentally about Singapore's voice in the international arena and how we keep our little red dot shining brightly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Why oppose something that should be done in Singapore's interests?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These reasons also track broadly why I disagree with the Opposition's broad points.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And having listened to the Opposition's aversions towards the amendments, I will end off giving my own personal view on the subject at hand from personal experience.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first point is this: we are a small country, yet we have done well.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are privileged to have gained respect around the globe for what we have built and for the people we have become.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is broadly on that basis that members of our Cabinet have been invited to participate in various international organisations and contribute generally globally.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, our Ministers have accepted these international roles to extend Singapore's standing abroad, so long as it is aligned with our national interests.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The third point, today, we are debating whether to extend this practice to the President as well.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This means that even as the President takes on a role, the Cabinet will continually consider if this role aids our national interests and how it helps Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fourth, this Bill is built on the backbone of our strong and established relationships with partners from around the world, as we seek to advance Singapore's national interests on the global stage and to gain international and commercial perspectives on issues that all countries face today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Being a part of such international groups and committees is essential as we look to bring Singapore forward.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Not only does it put Singapore on the map and allows us to contribute to issues beyond our borders, but we can gain insights into the considerations of other leaders in their respective countries and fields.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The commercial insight we gain helps us to keep abreast with how policies are affecting the economy and vice versa.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By understanding the ramifications in both the public and the private spheres, we are able to chart a better way forward for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fifth, over the years, our Cabinet has been invited to be a part of many international groups.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew, when he was Minister Mentor, took on such positions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He was a special advisor to Citigroup Inc. back in 2006, as well as being a part of the JP Morgan Chase International Council.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And, of course, President Tharman, when he was Senior Minister, took on several roles, including being a member of the WEF Board of Trustees, Co-chair of the GCEW and the G20 High Level Independent Panel on Financing the Global Commons for pandemic preparedness and response.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sixth, Mr Speaker, all these roles our Ministers have taken on have been appointments that have advanced Singapore's national interest and allowed our Cabinet to have a broader perspective, which they can utilise in governing Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Seventh, in the same way, to extend this role to our President, will serve Singapore well internationally and allow for greater global cooperation between us and the world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We can continue to build and strengthen relationships and significantly forged new ones, so that Singapore will always have a seat at the international table.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My ultimate point, before I go on to discuss the speeches before me, is one that comes from personal experience and deep personal belief.
