speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Perhaps I can give a personal account to drive home my point as to why international memberships are good for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just late last year, in 2022, I travelled with Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean on a Government trip to Egypt, and then to Paris, France.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Egypt, our objective was to get a sense of the security situation in North Africa, the region, southern Europe and the Middle East, and how movements there would impact Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We took a flight from Cairo to Paris.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our mission in Paris was to get a good sense of the Russia-Ukraine war, whether there was an end in sight – all in Singapore's interests.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the third day of our Paris leg, Senior Minister Teo attended the meetings of the TotalEnergies International Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the same hotel we were staying at were Senior Minister Teo's fellow industry advisory committee members from TotalEnergies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I met them socially at breakfast and spoke with them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The calibre of Senior Minister Teo's counterparts was exceptional.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That is my own honest, personal and real-life experience.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Captains of global industries, leaders in science and global experts in their fields.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That Senior Minister Teo was invited to be among such peers is both a credit to Singapore and to the Senior Minister.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I was left in no doubt, I repeat, I was left in no doubt that memberships at these high-level international bodies put Singapore on the map and advances our interests.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But equally important, it advances global interests and our common humanity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Is it any coincidence that Senior Minister Teo is also our Minister-in-charge of climate change?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: His perspectives add value to the global debate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While Senior Minister was at the TotalEnergies meetings, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) kept me occupied with bilateral meetings at the French Senate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: No time was wasted, and no resources were wasted; back-to-back meetings trying to advance Singapore's interests and global interests.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Like Mr Lee Kuan Yew, who was invited to international boards, or Senior Minister Teo, if our President is also held in such high esteem and his views are sought to advance a better world, why say no?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is a feather in the cap for Singapore, and what more Singapore gets a seat at the table.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And many a time, global goals – eradication of poverty, protection of water supplies and mitigating climate change – are in concert with, in other words, are consistent with our own national priorities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And that is why voting in favour of this constitutional amendment is a vote in favour of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are talking about the highest office of the land.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I listened carefully at the Opposition Members' speeches and had to say to myself, "I must respond to some of their arguments".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, let me start off with Mr Gerald Giam.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Gerald Giam has four points, or arguments rather, the hon Member uses some – and here, I speak through you, Mr Speaker, Sir – the hon Member has some reservations about some members of boards and committees who may not be in full integrity of the role they occupy on the board, given their other occupations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, Mr Giam's view is that Mr Tharman should be focused predominantly on inclusivity, arts and sports, and provide undivided attention to some of the declared objectives while he was on campaign.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Is arts, sports and inclusivity not also a global goal?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ought Singapore not be seen at boards and international meetings and conferences, promoting this global ideal?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If anything, there is economies of scale of attention to put forward this value.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Giam also says, "The Cabinet can say what he cannot say".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But it does not say that the Cabinet has to dictate what he has to say beyond what he cannot and therefore, there is free play, and we all know President Tharman, or most of us would know President Tharman as a man of his own thinking and deep integrity to his values.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I do not agree with the positions taken by my hon fellow Member Mr Gerald Giam.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Dennis Tan goes on to talk about how no other Head of State acts like this and there are only 24 hours in a day.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I think Members of this House would know that former Senior Minister Tharman, now President Tharman, packs a lot in, in 24 hours of his day.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I do not see there to be binary duties between what Mr Dennis Tan, or as I understood Mr Dennis Tan to say, is a domestic role and more of an international role.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He represents the state, and therefore, he has both to fulfil to the maximum of his ability and his or her talent the obligations at the international stage in addition to the domestic stage, which are not incompatible.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Dennis Tan then talks about what if there is a crisis and where should the President's attention be?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But if you look at some of the institutions that the President is now party to, they include the Independent Panel on Financing the Global Commons for Pandemic Preparedness and Response.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, if indeed we are talking about a crisis or a pandemic, ought it not be to Singapore's fillip, to Singapore's advantage, to Singapore's utility, that we have a person there, a reputable person, stating his own personal views, subject, of course, to the constraints and fetters offered by Cabinet, if any?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Leong says there is a violation in what we are doing today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I hope that puts in perspective the good faith nature of what we are doing today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is not a "may", if I read it correctly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And let us hope that never comes to it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, we are not in a situation of a binary choice where we have to say, "Look, no memberships because we do not want our President being overly distracted by international duties" or "we want a largely domestic President to be on the ground".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim ended off with really what was a political point, and what was the political point of today's debate among the Opposition Members of Parliament, in my humble view – which was a political point, "Thank goodness that we have Members in this House, that if we had enough Members, we could railroad and prevent this amendment from going through if we had the one-third.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I think Mr de Souza is making a strawman argument.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: He is arguing that the WP does not think that our President and Ministers should sit on international boards.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What I did say is, I accept that the President may sometimes take up roles in international organisations in his official capacity, in order to advance Singapore's international standing and advance our national interests.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We have no issue with him taking up these roles in his official capacity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What we disagree with him, is him taking up these roles in his private capacity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I think Mr de Souza has not addressed that in his speech.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the Deputy Prime Minister already clarified that these international organisations are happy to have our President and Ministers in their official capacity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, I do not see what the issue is.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I am afraid the Member is incorrect on two counts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The first is that the private bodies see the elevation of Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam as the President, as Head of State, to be an advantage to their organisations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But as I understood it, they did not want him to be just stating what the Government's position on things would be.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And this was never contemplated in the Constitution, because the Constitution always had official capacity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: They did not sneak it under the carpet and said, bygones be bygones.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Just carry on with official capacity and let the President say what he wants to say in private capacity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: No, that would be wrong, even if nobody found out.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The Attorney-General said, "Look, based on the tools, the framework and the mechanics of the Constitution, this may not – this may run into a little bit of trouble.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, why do we not allow memberships via private capacities, but fetter them?" Fetter them by Cabinet, and that is why we have Article 22C.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, it was out of an abundance of caution that we are doing what we are doing today.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: He said, but Mr Tharman has been on these Boards in his official capacity all this time.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong has confirmed that all these positions that he is currently on, are in his official capacity and he has been speaking his mind all this time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Mr Tharman is now the Head of State.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And therefore, we have to have a structure, predictability, a framework in order to resolve what could be internationally prickly situations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And if you look at the explanatory statement, it states very clearly under Article 22C what the Cabinet can advise the President to do.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In deciding whether to give his concurrence, the President is not subject to a time limit.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And the President must relinquish the office if so advised by the Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, Mr Tharman has now been elevated to Head of State.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And this provides, I think, both His Excellency and the regulators in the form of the Cabinet to have a very predictable framework to deal with these issues.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And let us not throw the baby out with the bathwater.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: There are issues that are facing the globe which our Ministers and also the President have unique, deep insights to contribute towards.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, do we put a roadblock or do we find a workable solution?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And in the Singapore way, we find a workable solution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, let me first put that on the record.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, if I heard Mr de Souza correctly, he suggests that one impetus for this Bill is that it was to accommodate, potentially, the concerns of these international organisations, about the independence of our potential representatives were we to send them there.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps I should ask the question: what does it say about us as a nation, as a sovereign nation, if we are amending the highest law of the land, just so that we can potentially appease the desires of international organisations?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If you are not at the table, you are on the menu.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, when you get invited to these organisations, they speak well of Singapore, they speak well of the person who has been invited.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The door is ajar, Singapore's interests can be presented by way of osmosis and the whole ecosystem, in the boardroom or the committee room, you get a sense of each continent's political difficulties and economic difficulties.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We are not pandering to the requests of international organisations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The fact that people who I have mentioned – Mr Lee Kuan Yew, Senior Minister Teo, other esteemed Cabinet Ministers and Senior Minister Tharman – continue to be sought after, after years in Government, speaks well that they are relevant.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But they want not just the official line.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If there is room to share from their own experience and their own wealth of knowledge, what they have been through, how they think things can pan out, not just for Singapore, but for the world and for the region, why veto that?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How can that be construed as us pandering to international organisations when it is a feather in the cap to actually be invited in the first place?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And then set down rules as to what can or cannot be done, so that the international organisations know the rules of engagement and so do we, both on His Excellency's Head of State side and on Cabinet side.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, I turned it on its head and say we are not pandering.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We should be honoured and humbled, and accept, as far as possible, subject to national interests.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When I listen to the debate, especially the points raised by Member Christopher de Souza.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can I make a clarification to the Deputy Prime Minister?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You can raise your clarification with respect to his opening speech, but later, he will have a chance to give his closing speech.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Yes, because I would like to develop further the issue about official capacity and private capacity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I want to make one clarification with the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, many of the questions from Members, if you had listened carefully to my opening remarks, were already addressed in my opening remarks.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But nevertheless, let me go through some of these points again.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, on why this does not apply to the Prime Minister.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have got the President, we have got Ministers, but why not the Prime Minister?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this is not relevant to the Prime Minister.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, what is the status of President Tharman's current appointments?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The present status are the four appointments which I have highlighted just now.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They are appointments in the official capacity and they are not unconstitutional.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They are made in accordance with the advice and support of the Cabinet.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These are not full-time appointments; these are not executive appointments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They are roles as Board of Trustees, advisory roles; so, it is quite different from some of the examples that Mr Giam had cited earlier too.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Third, on the issue of backdating, I had addressed that too.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Backdating, as Assoc Prof Jamus Lim correctly said, should be done sparingly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is really the exception rather than the norm and we do it very, very rarely.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because backdating upsets expectations and prejudices individuals who rely on the existing law.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And so, if you backdate, then the ones who had relied on existing law may well be prejudiced.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There were several Members who asked how the Government would assess invitations for the President or Ministers to participate in these international bodies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Then, you might ask, what do we mean by "national interest"?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In general, the President or Minister's participation should be helpful in advancing Singapore's standing and interests on the international stage.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There should be benefits, be it direct or indirect, to Singapore as a whole or the Government agency which oversees the sector that the organisation operates in.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There might also be clear outcomes we want to help progress through these arrangements.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, the President or the Minister's participation could help advance views that are aligned to Singapore's outlook and approach on issues to help shape the global agenda in areas that are critical to Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These benefits could also take the form of staying plugged into global discussions on topics salient to Singapore or generating mindshare for Singapore among influential thought leaders and networks.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, that is what we would say broadly is in the national interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But what I want to reiterate, and it is important and a substantive point to reiterate here, undertaking this role in a private capacity does not mean that the President or the Minister is somehow doing some extra-curricular activity, something that is outside of his work duties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: When the President serves in this capacity, he is contributing to his national responsibilities, and he is undertaking his presidential duties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As Mr Christopher de Souza correctly said, the presidential office is not a President for domestic or international, it is a President serving both domestic and international interests.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A key role of the President is as Singapore's top diplomat.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: International dimensions are part and parcel of the President's role and how he contributes to Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this is not a trade-off, as though doing this is outside of his presidential duties; they are integral to his presidential duties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Another misunderstanding from what I have heard so far is a confusion between private views and private interests.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A lot of the comments suggest that when the President serves in his private capacity, he is serving in his private interests.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are allowing him, when he serves under this new clause, to serve in a way that allows him to contribute his private views, subject to safeguards, as I mentioned in my earlier speech.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Beyond that, we allow him to contribute independently to these organisations in his private capacity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But when he does so, he does so in the national interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, he is not serving in his private interests, he is serving in the national interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I hope that clarifies what this envisages, this provision allows the President and Ministers to do.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Approving an appointment, when the Cabinet agrees to the President or to a Minister undertaking these assignments, we are doing this for the national interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are doing this so that the President can project Singapore’s influence and strengthen our networks in the world, fulfilling his presidential duties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Approving an appointment in its private capacity is a way for us to facilitate the President acting independently to achieve the aims of the organisations, subject to the necessary safeguards of our national interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: You could say – and I think, Mr Gerald Giam and Mr Leong Mun Wai asked just now – this is the first time we are doing this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Previously, Ministers have served in organisations with the approval of the Prime Minister and when they did so, they did so in their private capacity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There was no legal impediment for Ministers to do so, but now, we are dealing with a novel situation where it comes to the President.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The President had in the past served in international organisations in his official capacity before.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And the Government could very well, as an alternative to what we are discussing today, have said, "Maybe we should just allow the President to continue holding the international appointments in his official capacity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: After all, had been done before, Dr Tan had served so why not continue to do so with President Tharman?" And, indeed, as I mentioned in my opening remarks, this was our thinking.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we only came to the realisation after President Tharman's election, as we were deliberating over the matter.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We could have said we will continue with this arrangement, let him serve in his official capacity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, we might even have given him latitude to express some independent views while contributing to these organisations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: AGC said this is not expressly prohibited by law and if we had taken this approach, people would be none the wiser.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Opposition would not even have objected to it, I assume, from what I gathered from Mr Gerald Giam just now.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our conclusion was that this will not be ideal for us, for Singapore; and neither will it be ideal for the international organisations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because the nature and parameters of the President's involvement would be unclear.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Is he speaking for Singapore or is he speaking for himself?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, when I heard some of the speeches from Opposition Members and their opposition to this Bill, with phrases suggesting that this is not proper, that somehow it is unconstitutional and	 that this is some violation of established principles – this is completely unfounded.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Let us not use this technical language to camouflage political grandstanding.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Let us come back to the substance of what this is about.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ultimately, this is about Singapore, or as Mr Leong Mun Wai would say, "This is for country, for people".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we have to ask ourselves the substance of these provisions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Do they bring benefits to Singapore and Singaporeans?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is what the substance of it is.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And from the Government's point of view, the provisions are very clear.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will enable our little red dot to shine brightly on the international stage.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On that basis, if that is the case, how about resourcing support for the President when he undertakes these international roles in his private capacity or for that matter when a Minister does so?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Based on the explanation I said just now, precisely because when the President serves, he is not serving in his private interest, he is serving in the national interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Therefore, the resourcing support is no different from how the Government supports the President when he undertakes an official trip.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: He contributes his private views to these organisations, but he is going on these trips on the basis of national interest, not for his private business.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the President’s case, this will include staff support to review the materials, provide briefs for the meetings he attends, as well as funding for the travel costs of President and his delegation as and when there are international meetings.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In other words, this is like a working trip; no different from any other working trips the President or the Minister undertakes in the national interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, remember, private views are not the same as private interests.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This Bill allows him to express private views but still serve in the national interest, doing duties that are integral and part and parcel of presidential duties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Then there were questions of possible conflicts of interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These could arise, for example, if the foreign or international organisations were to take positions that are different from the Government or if a President or Minister were to take steps that are detrimental to the nation’s interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But such potential conflicts of interest or questions of conflict will be considered in deciding whether or not to support an appointment in the first place.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If the questions of conflict do arise later on in the course of an appointment, the individual can take steps to remove the conflict, for example, by recusing himself or herself from a particular decision that would conflict with their official duties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Cabinet can also advise the President accordingly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Prime Minister can likewise instruct a Minister.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If there are serious questions of conflict that cannot be resolved, the President or the Minister would have to relinquish the appointment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If necessary, Cabinet would advise the President to do so, and the Prime Minister would instruct a Minister.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And if the President, as I think, Mr Dennis Tan says, intentionally refuses to follow the Cabinet's advice, then that would be grounds for removal and there are procedures set out for such removals.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is already the current arrangement for Ministers, and it will continue to be so under the new framework.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Again, Cabinet will advise the President, and the Prime Minister will instruct Ministers, to this effect.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is having accepted that the President's roles cover both domestic and international, but I suppose there will be questions asked about emphasis and bandwidth and how you spend the time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And so, in assessing invitations to the President, the Cabinet will consider, among other things, the commitments expected by this international role.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Cabinet will also consider the meeting load and travel demands, and whether these are reasonable.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this will ensure that the President’s holding of these roles remains to Singapore’s benefit and will not, in any way, affect his ability to exercise the rest of his constitutional duties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Prime Minister will likewise do the same for roles involving Ministers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the end of the day, it would not be in the national interest for the President or a Minister to take on external appointments that affect their ability to perform their official duties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: All assessments made by Cabinet will carefully weigh any potential bandwidth concerns against the potential benefit the appointments will bring.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, Sir, at the end of the day, I think we have to come back to the substance and merits of what this amendment Bill is about.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Do we want the President to take on these international roles in his independent and private capacity, when it is in the national interest?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And if so, do we want to put in place a proper legal and governing framework for such an arrangement rather than to pretend, fudge the issue and just operate in this ambiguous, grey zone without being upfront?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want to have a principled framework to govern how the President and Ministers take on international appointments in their private capacities, where required by the national interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we want to do so sooner rather than later.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have identified the issue, it came up, we looked at it and we settled on a solution which is being proposed in this House.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The sooner we get this done, the sooner the President can embark on his engagements under a clear constitutional framework.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is nothing to be gained by delay.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is out of an abundance of caution because he has been appointed in an official basis, but he has decided not to attend any formal meetings.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Should Parliament pass this amendment Bill, then the new framework will be in place and President Tharman will be able to attend future meetings under this new governing arrangement.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And, indeed, there are upcoming meetings, including the G30 Winter Plenary in New York next week.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We know that the Constitution is a living document.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It should not be amended frivolously, but it also cannot stay static.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It has to evolve as our needs change over the years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And indeed, it was Cabinet that assessed the need to move this constitutional amendment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We agreed that it would be a positive and necessary structural change and would increase the ability of individuals to contribute to Singapore while ensuring the relevant safeguards and ensuring greater accountability.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our survival depends on us being able to respond to the changing global landscape and to deliver value to the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Opportunities to take up office in respected international institutions where we can actively contribute to shaping global norms – these do not come by all the time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is not as though these institutions will say, "Look, any Singaporean also can come and serve in my organisation." But the few occasions when these invitations come by, I think we should treasure them.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And this is indeed how we have built strong relationships with other countries, while safeguarding our interests and ensuring that our voices are heard on the global stage.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I cannot emphasise how much Singapore has gained because our top officials are regularly tapped on by international bodies and foreign governments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And this was the case from our founding generation of leaders.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Dr Goh Keng Swee, for example, was tapped on by the Chinese government in 1985 to advise them on the setting up of the Special Economic Zones in China.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: He was then Deputy Chairman of both the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and GIC.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: While he was Deputy Prime Minister, he was also tapped on by the Sri Lankan government to advise them on the restructuring of the economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Chinese and Sri Lankan government did not ask Dr Goh because they wanted him to act in the interest of the Singapore Government in China or Sri Lanka, obviously.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They asked him because they knew his record as the architect of Singapore's economy and hope that he would be able to help them.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Prime Minister then Mr Lee Kuan Yew readily agreed to Dr Goh playing these roles because they brought credit to Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They underlined our usefulness to the world and projected our influence abroad.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Likewise, these international bodies are not asking President Tharman to continue playing a role in their organisations because they want him to represent Singapore's views or the views of the Singapore Government.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They are asking him because they know his record in the Singapore Government and hope he would be able to give sound advice on global issues.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And it also reflects how this Government works – to deal with issues squarely to be upfront and transparent and to act in a way that is consistent with sound legal and governance principles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I will ask the WP and the PSP, having heard my explanations to reconsider your positions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is no need to oppose for the sake of opposition.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is no need to oppose something that will clearly advance Singapore's interests and bring benefits to Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In some ways, Singapore is at the stage of our development where our national interests are becoming more closely intertwined with global interests.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we need to find ways to achieve this intertwining, and this Bill is one of the ways to achieve this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, let us all, hopefully everyone in this House will agree, give your support for the Bill, do our part to strengthen Singapore's voice on the international stage, to add to our participation in influential global forums and to ensure that this little red dot continues to shine brightly in a dark and troubled world.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have two more clarifications for the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One, is the current position taken up by Senior Minister Teo in TotalEnergies in his private capacity?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Two, if, in the past, Ministers had been taking up positions in their private capacity and so, now for the President, the Cabinet is being advised by the AGC that there are some issues.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think to be a responsible Opposition, we still want to understand what are the issues that the AGC has raised?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Is it pertaining to the fact that: one, that the Cabinet does not have complete control over the President's appointments and that is why we need this Bill?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Or is it because there are certain appointments, just like what the WP and us are saying, where he can perform his role in his official capacity, that should be no problem.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But if certain appointments require a private capacity, what are those appointments?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I seek the Deputy Prime Minister’s clarification, please?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Senior Minister Teo or, for that matter, the many examples I cited before him – Dr Goh Keng Swee and other Ministers – were acting in their private capacity in these international organisations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is because they were authorised to do so by the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is no legal impediment for the Prime Minister to so authorise Ministers to act in their private capacity, subject to safeguards and principles, which I have just described.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And so, this has been happening not just with Senior Minister Teo, but even way back with Dr Goh and many other examples.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, you say, why can you not do it for the President?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And as I have explained, the Prime Minister cannot authorise the President to do likewise.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why we debated, and we thought about it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: One option, as I described just now, was for us to, rather than authorise the President to act in his private capacity, allow the President to serve in his official capacity, but with some latitude to express his private views.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And AGC said that is not clearly, expressly prohibited.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That was what I tried to explain in my speech – not ideal.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It leads us into new grey and ambiguous areas because no one will know whether what the President says is reflecting his personal views or the Singapore Government's views, official views, what is it?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we prefer not to operate like that in such an ambiguous manner.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we prefer to do this in a principled manner, with a clear governing framework, hence the amendments before this House.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any further clarifications for Deputy Prime Minister Wong?

text: Before I proceed to start the electronic voting, may I remind Members that they are to be seated at their designated seats and should only start to vote when the voting buttons on the arm rest start to blink.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Now, Sir, I beg to move, "That the Bill be now read a Third time."

speaker: Mr Speaker

Pursuant to Article 5(2) of the Constitution, a vote is taken to ascertain that the Third Reading of the Bill is supported by the votes of not less than two-thirds of the total number of Elected and Non-Constituency Members of Parliament, which is 60 Members.
